Then a point of light appeared beyond the lunar edge, too bright to be a [[distant]] star. The rest of the crew were asleep. Imani checked the navigation display, but the object did not appear on any [[chart]]. Outside, the light [[shifted]].

The first time the station went quiet, Mei thought the [[engines]] had stopped. She ran to the observation deck and felt their [[low]] vibration through the floor. Mara walked beneath the trees with her hands in the [[pockets]] of her coat. The path was [[narrow]] and dark with rain, its shallow [[puddles]] holding the pale sky in broken pieces. Beech leaves, copper-brown and slick, had [[gathered]] in the hollows. Her boots [[pressed]] them flat with a soft, papery sound. Somewhere ahead, water moved over stones. She could not see the stream yet, but she followed its steady [[murmur]] between the trunks.

The forest was quiet in the way a room is quiet when someone else is still in it. A robin [[shifted]] in the [[brambles]], and a blackbird [[called]] once from the low branches. When Mara stopped, the birds stopped too. She waited, breathing in the cool smell of wet bark and earth. Then a squirrel [[raced]] up an oak, its claws clicking against the [[trunk]], and the woods resumed their small [[movements]].

At the stream, the path crossed a footbridge made from two old [[planks]]. Water [[slipped]] beneath it, clear over the shallows and dark where the bank folded into shadow. Moss had [[softened]] the stones. A [[fallen]] branch lay across the far edge, caught there by the [[current]], and tiny leaves turned slowly in an eddy behind it. Mara leaned over the rail. A few minnows [[flickered]] above the gravel, vanished, and returned farther downstream.

She had walked this route in every [[season]], though never often enough to feel that she knew it completely. The forest changed its [[shape]] without changing its place. Its trees held the same [[ground]]; its paths climbed the same [[slopes]]. Yet light, weather and the lives moving among the [[roots]] remade it month by month.

In winter, the stream ran higher. Rain [[travelled]] through the soil and gathered in the [[valley]], pushing past the bridge with a quicker, heavier voice. Frost [[silvered]] the grass at the path’s edge. On cold mornings, branches clicked together overhead, and every [[footprint]] appeared sharply in the mud before the next shower softened it. The bare canopy let more light reach the forest floor, but the light was thin and [[brief]]. By mid-afternoon, the trunks stood in long [[shadows]].

Many animals responded to winter by doing less. Hedgehogs slept in [[nests]] of leaves and grass, protected from the cold beneath fallen branches or inside [[sheltered]] banks. Their stillness [[conserved]] energy when beetles and worms were [[scarce]]. Bats settled into hidden places to [[hibernate]], their bodies quiet, their breathing slowed. Other animals stayed active, but changed their routines. Deer fed when the woods were calm, browsing on twigs and the last tough leaves. Foxes travelled farther in search of food, leaving neat [[tracks]] across snow or soft ground. A mouse might remain almost invisible beneath the leaf litter, gathering seeds and moving through narrow spaces where larger animals could not follow.

Winter did not empty the forest. It made life [[harder]] to see. A woodpecker [[tapped]] at a tree, testing the bark for [[insects]]. A flock of tits [[searched]] the branches for eggs and larvae. Under the snow, beetles and other small creatures waited out the cold in the soil. Even the fallen leaves mattered: they formed a [[blanket]] that held [[warmth]] and moisture, and a hiding place for the smallest lives.

Then the days [[lengthened]]. At first, spring seemed to arrive in details rather than events: a [[brighter]] morning, a line of green at the edge of a ditch, the [[swelling]] buds of a hazel. Water still shone in the hollows, but the ground began to [[soften]]. The first flowers [[opened]] where sunlight reached the forest floor before the trees leafed out. Their brief window was important. Once the [[canopy]] filled, little light would reach them.

Birdsong grew more varied. Some birds had spent the winter elsewhere and returned to claim [[territories]]; others had stayed, waiting for insects to [[emerge]]. They carried [[twigs]] and grasses into hedges and forks in the branches, building nests out of sight. The woodland seemed full of [[errands]]. A blackbird [[tugged]] at a worm. A wren disappeared into a tangle of roots. Near the stream, frogs gathered in [[shallow]] pools to lay their eggs, where the water warmed sooner than the deeper current.

For animals raising young, spring brought both plenty and risk. Insects [[hatched]] in greater numbers, providing food for [[chicks]] that needed frequent feeding. But nests were [[exposed]] to cold rain, [[predators]] and sudden changes in temperature. A parent bird could spend much of the day carrying food back and forth, watching the surrounding branches between trips. Beneath the brambles, a deer’s [[newborn]] fawn lay very still while its mother moved away to feed. Stillness and [[camouflage]] were its first protections.

By early summer, leaves had closed overhead. The forest floor cooled beneath the [[dense]] shade, while the clearings warmed in the sun. Ferns [[unfolded]] along the stream banks; grasses brushed Mara’s knees where the path [[widened]]. The air carried the smell of [[crushed]] leaves and warm pine. Insects [[hummed]] above the brambles. A dragonfly hovered over a puddle, then [[darted]] away so quickly that Mara saw only its blue flash.

The animals’ lives filled the long days. Young birds tested their [[wings]] among low branches. Squirrels [[gathered]] food, carrying nuts away from the trees that had dropped them. Badgers [[emerged]] at [[dusk]] to search for worms, roots and insects. Fox [[cubs]] played near their den before the adults led them farther from it. Each creature used a different part of the forest, and often at a different time. The birds worked in the [[canopy]]; mice travelled beneath it. Deer crossed open ground at dawn and dusk, when they could see danger and remain less visible themselves.

Summer also brought its pressures. A dry spell could [[shrink]] pools and leave the stream low among its stones. Fish [[crowded]] into the [[deeper]] channels, where the water stayed cooler. Small mammals had to travel farther for water, while plants [[competed]] for moisture through the roots beneath them. The forest’s shade helped, but could not [[prevent]] every loss. A storm might break a [[heavy]] branch, or wind might bring down a whole tree. In the gap left behind, sunlight reached the ground and gave new plants a chance.

By autumn, the path was once again [[strewn]] with leaves. Some turned yellow before they fell; others held their green until a sharp night [[loosened]] them. The forest smelled of damp wood, fungi and fruit. Brambles offered dark [[berries]], and acorns dropped into the grass with small, solid [[knocks]]. Mara heard them land but did not always see them. A jay was quicker. It carried acorns away and hid them in the soil, storing food for the colder months. Some would be eaten later; some would be [[forgotten]], and might grow into oaks.

Other animals prepared in their own ways. Squirrels built [[stores]] of nuts. Dormice fed heavily before entering winter sleep. Deer grew thicker [[coats]], while birds gathered in [[flocks]] and made longer [[journeys]] in search of [[milder]] weather. For many creatures, autumn was a narrow bridge between abundance and [[scarcity]]. The fruit and seeds available now could determine how well they survived the months ahead.

Mara reached the old gate as daylight began to [[fade]]. Behind her, the stream kept moving beneath the bridge. Leaves [[settled]] along the path, covering [[tracks]] made only hours before. Somewhere in the trees, a fox called; farther off, wings beat through the [[darkening]] canopy. The forest had no single season, not really. Winter was already gathering inside the autumn seeds; next spring waited in buds [[sealed]] against the cold. Mara stepped through the gate, while the woods continued around her, storing, [[shedding]], resting and beginning again.

Autumn is perhaps the richest season of all. Tables [[groan]] under the [[weight]] of [[shiny]] apples, fat orange pumpkins and baskets of wild mushrooms. The honey seller returns with [[jars]] of dark, sticky honey that [[glow]] in the low sunlight. There is a [[hint]] of woodsmoke in the air, along with the comforting scent of freshly baked bread and cinnamon buns from the bakery stall.

By July, the market is [[bursting]] with life and colour. At eight in the morning it is already warm, and by two in the afternoon the stone square can feel like an [[oven]], sometimes reaching thirty [[degrees]] or more. Traders put up wide [[umbrellas]] and [[spray]] their fruit with water to keep it looking fresh. Dogs lie panting in any patch of [[shade]] they can find.

By late November, the rain often arrives. Drops [[drum]] loudly on the canvas roofs, and shoppers [[shelter]] under umbrellas, stepping carefully around [[puddles]] that [[reflect]] the grey sky. The traders are tired now, but they are still [[cheerful]]. They know that soon the fairy lights will go up, the smell of chestnuts will return, and the market will begin its long, [[familiar]] circle once again.

By May, the market feels much [[lighter]]. The mornings are cool, but the afternoon sun [[warms]] the backs of people waiting at the bread stall. Jackets become thinner, and some visitors arrive in short [[sleeves]]. There are more flowers now: tall [[stems]], small bunches of herbs and plants in pots. Their fresh, sweet smell mixes with warm bread and the [[earthy]] scent of newly [[washed]] vegetables.

By mid-morning, the market is busy but quiet. Shoppers move quickly, keeping their hands in their [[pockets]] until they need to choose something. Dark winter coats fill the [[narrow]] paths between stalls. The smell of hot coffee [[drifts]] from a small van, mixing with [[damp]] wool, cold earth and the clean, strong scent of oranges. Somewhere, a loose sign [[rattles]] in the [[wind]].

By October, the air has a [[crisp]] edge. Leaves blow between the stalls, catching against table legs before [[tumbling]] into the corners of the square. People arrive in coats, some carrying [[scarves]] over their arms in case the afternoon warms. The smell of roasted nuts becomes [[noticeable]] near the entrance. On wet days, the whole market seems [[darker]], but baskets of orange [[squash]] and red apples keep the centre bright.

December fills the square with colour again. Small lights hang above the stalls, [[glowing]] softly as evening approaches. Visitors wear [[thick]] coats, bright hats and gloves, and many carry gifts [[tucked]] beneath their arms. The smell of cinnamon, pine and warm pastry [[drifts]] through the crowd. The market is busiest near the [[centre]], where people pause to look at [[decorations]] and choose food for winter meals.

Every Saturday, the old square in the centre of town turns into a [[market]]. The stalls arrive before [[sunrise]], carried in small vans and pushed into [[neat]] rows across the [[cobblestones]]. The market has stood here for over a hundred years, and it changes with every [[season]], like a living thing that [[breathes]] in and out with the weather.

In April, rain arrives in short, [[sudden]] showers. Visitors lift [[umbrellas]] as dark clouds cross the square, then close them again when the sun returns. Drops [[gather]] on the stall roofs and fall in a [[steady]] line at the edges. The smell of wet stone [[rises]] from the ground. Beneath bright umbrellas, shoppers [[compare]] fruit, carrying bags in one hand and keeping the other free to hold their coats.

In August, the square seems to hold the day’s [[heat]]. Even the morning air feels [[warm]], and the stone walls keep the sun long after it has moved behind the buildings. People seek [[shade]] wherever they can find it. Stallholders [[arrange]] their produce carefully, turning [[delicate]] fruit away from direct sunlight. The market smells of ripe melons, herbs and dust, with a hint of sharp [[vinegar]] from a pickle stall.

In February, little has changed, but the days are beginning to grow longer. The morning still feels near [[freezing]], though sunlight sometimes reaches the [[rooftops]] before the stalls are open. A thin [[mist]] hangs over the vegetables. Purple cabbages, [[muddy]] potatoes and bundles of carrots look unusually [[bright]] against the grey ground. Regular visitors know where each stall stands and follow the same careful [[route]].

In January, the market square lies beneath a [[pale]] winter sky. At dawn, [[frost]] covers the paving stones, and the air feels [[sharp]] against the face. The first stallholders arrive wrapped in thick coats, scarves and woolly hats. Their [[breath]] rises in small clouds as they lift boxes from vans. The metal [[frames]] of the stalls shine with cold, and the canvas roofs [[snap]] whenever the wind pushes through.

In January, the market wakes slowly. At seven in the morning, the air is sharp and [[bitter]], often just below freezing, and frost [[sparkles]] on the canvas roofs. Traders [[stamp]] their feet and blow into their hands. Their breath hangs in small white [[clouds]]. Many of them wear thick woolly hats, [[fingerless]] gloves and several [[layers]] of old jumpers under heavy coats.

In July, the heat [[settles]] over the market before noon. The air grows warm beneath the canvas roofs, and the space between stalls feels [[crowded]] and still. Ice [[melts]] quickly in cool boxes. Peaches, cherries and plums shine in neat [[piles]], their [[sweet]] smell drawing people closer. Some visitors carry wide hats or hold bags above their heads to [[block]] the sun as they cross the open square.

In November, daylight [[fades]] early, and the market grows quieter towards the end of the afternoon. The first visitors arrive beneath low [[clouds]], their coats [[buttoned]] against the cold. Stallholders work with [[gloved]] hands, rubbing them together between tasks. Steam rises from a food stall, carrying the smell of [[soup]] and baked potatoes across the wet paving. People gather around it for [[warmth]] before continuing their shopping.

In the late afternoon, the heat slowly [[softens]]. The light turns honey-coloured, and long [[shadows]] stretch across the cobblestones. Traders [[fan]] themselves with pieces of cardboard and start to count their money. The square smells of [[crushed]] fruit, warm dust and sun cream. Even after the last stalls have [[packed]] away, people stay, sitting on the fountain steps and chatting until the evening air finally [[cools]].

June brings long, bright days. The market opens in clear early light, and the metal poles cast narrow [[shadows]] across the square. By [[midday]], the paving stones are warm, and stallholders place bottles of water within [[reach]]. Visitors wear sunglasses, light shirts and loose summer [[dresses]]. They walk more slowly than they did in winter, stopping to [[taste]] fruit or admire colourful [[cloth]] spread across a table.

March brings an [[uncertain]] warmth. One morning may be cold enough for [[gloves]]; the next may feel almost [[mild]] by lunchtime. The first spring flowers appear in [[buckets]] near the entrance, their yellow and white heads shaking in the [[breeze]]. People begin to leave their heavy coats unbuttoned. Children notice the flowers first, while older shoppers pause to [[examine]] the new green vegetables and the prices beside them.

On the final mornings of the year, the market returns to its winter [[rhythm]]. The air is cold, the stones are [[damp]], and the roofs [[shake]] in the wind. A few early visitors move quickly, while others [[wander]] without hurry, studying [[familiar]] stalls. The seasons have changed the produce, the clothes and the sounds of the square. Yet the market remains a [[meeting]] place, shaped each day by weather, work and the people who pass through it.

September arrives quietly. The tourists [[disappear]] almost overnight, and the mornings gain a fresh, [[crisp]] edge. At dawn it might be only eight or nine [[degrees]], though the afternoons can still be pleasantly [[mild]]. Leaves from the plane trees begin to fall, [[crunching]] under people’s boots and collecting in golden [[piles]] around the legs of the stalls.

September brings a gentler light. The mornings are [[cooler]], and a thin layer of [[mist]] sometimes rests above the square before the sun [[burns]] it away. Visitors begin to wear light [[jumpers]] again. The displays change too: apples, pears and pumpkins appear beside the final summer [[berries]]. Their colours are deeper and calmer than the bright reds and yellows of July, matching the slower [[pace]] of the season.

Spring brings new faces too. Students in [[denim]] jackets and bright trainers [[wander]] between the stalls, laughing and taking [[photos]] for social media. Young parents push [[buggies]] and stop to let their toddlers point at the ducks painted on the toy seller’s van. There is a feeling of [[optimism]] everywhere, as if the whole town has just woken up from a long, heavy [[sleep]].

Summer is a [[feast]] for the senses. Strawberries, cherries and [[ripe]] peaches shine in their wooden boxes, while wasps [[buzz]] greedily around them. The smell of [[sizzling]] sausages and spicy street food [[floats]] from the food trucks at the edge of the square. A street musician plays a cheerful tune on his accordion, and somewhere, a child is always [[begging]] for an ice cream.

The flower stall becomes the [[heart]] of the market. Buckets [[overflow]] with daffodils, tulips and bunches of [[fragrant]] lilac. Their perfume mixes with the earthy smell of seedlings and fresh [[compost]] from the garden stall, where keen gardeners examine tiny tomato plants as if they were [[precious]] jewels. Young herbs like mint and basil fill the air with a clean, green [[freshness]].

The smells of winter are warm and [[comforting]]. Chestnuts [[crackle]] in a black iron [[pan]], and the sweet, smoky scent [[drifts]] across the square. Nearby, a woman sells hot apple juice from a [[steaming]] pot, full of cinnamon and cloves. The vegetable stalls are piled high with muddy potatoes, purple cabbages and knobbly [[parsnips]], the honest food that keeps people going through the cold months.

The summer crowd is the most [[varied]] of the year. Tourists in sun hats and [[sandals]] move slowly, studying maps and [[admiring]] handmade jewellery. Teenagers in shorts and sunglasses gather in [[noisy]] groups. There are always a few confident bargain hunters, who [[argue]] cheerfully about prices, and a few dreamers, who drift from stall to stall without buying anything at all, simply enjoying the [[atmosphere]].

The summer visitors have different [[habits]]. Some arrive early, before the heat becomes [[tiring]], and leave with heavy [[baskets]]. Others come later, strolling in small groups and taking [[photographs]] of the bright displays. There are families with young children, cyclists in sports clothes and older people who know many of the stallholders by sight. The busiest paths are [[lively]] with footsteps, the scrape of crates and the [[rustle]] of paper bags.

The visitors change once again. People wear [[cosy]] scarves, ankle boots and knitted [[cardigans]] in [[shades]] of mustard, rust and forest green, almost matching the leaves. Families come to choose [[pumpkins]] for Halloween, and serious cooks search for the perfect [[ingredients]] for soups and stews. Shoppers move more slowly than in summer, as if they want to make the most of the gentle, fading [[light]].

The winter visitors are mostly locals with a [[purpose]]. Elderly [[couples]] walk arm in arm, checking prices carefully before they buy. A retired teacher in a long camel coat comes every week for the same [[loaf]] of rye bread. By midday the [[temperature]] rarely climbs above four or five degrees, and most shoppers [[hurry]] home, their cheeks pink and their bags [[heavy]].

Then, in March, something [[shifts]]. The mornings are still [[chilly]], but the light arrives earlier, pale and golden, and birds begin to [[chatter]] in the plane trees around the square. By late April, the [[temperature]] at noon can reach fifteen degrees, and people slowly [[unbutton]] their coats. Some [[brave]] souls even sit outside the café with their faces turned towards the sun.

Through every [[season]], one thing stays the same. Whether the square is [[frozen]], flowering, baking or soaked, the market [[remains]] a place where people meet, notice each other and share the simple [[pleasure]] of buying something good. It is not just a place to [[shop]]. It is the [[beating]] heart of the town.

A teacher’s [[footsteps]] approached from the far end, quick and [[firm]]. Leo moved to the side, shoulders drawing in as a group [[hurried]] past. The corridor smelled stronger here, where wet jackets had been hung on [[hooks]] beside the classroom doors. Beneath that [[damp]] scent was the chalky smell of paper and pencil shavings, [[familiar]] enough to remind him of his old classroom.

As he turned the corner, the school appeared. It was [[enormous]]. Compared with his tiny primary school, with its single [[playground]] and its friendly painted walls, this place looked like a [[factory]]. Three [[storeys]] of red brick and glass rose above a wide car park. Through the black [[iron]] gates [[poured]] hundreds of students, and their noise reached Leo long before he reached them.

At exactly half past eight, a bell rang. It was not a [[gentle]] ring but a long, metallic [[scream]] that seemed to [[shake]] the windows. Immediately, the crowd began to move. Like water rushing down a [[drain]], the students [[funnelled]] towards the main doors, and Leo had no choice but to go with them. His heart was [[hammering]]. His palms felt hot and sticky.

At the [[entrance]], the movement seemed to gather speed. Students passed through the glass doors in a [[steady]] stream, bringing with them the smell of rain, warm clothes and the faint [[sweetness]] of shampoo. A bell sounded somewhere inside. Its clear, sharp [[note]] cut through the [[rumble]] of buses and the rustle of coats, making Leo’s stomach [[tighten]].

At the top, he found Room 12. Through the open door, he could see rows of [[desks]], a whiteboard and a [[display]] of maps. Several students had already chosen seats, [[arranging]] pencil cases and books in front of them. Their faces looked [[calm]], or perhaps only busy. Leo paused outside, suddenly aware of the new shoes [[pinching]] his heels and the paper timetable [[trembling]] slightly in his hand.

Because Hillcrest had no [[uniform]], the [[variety]] of clothes amazed him. A tall girl [[strode]] past in a long black coat and heavy boots. Two boys in [[matching]] football shirts [[kicked]] a can between them. One student wore a yellow [[raincoat]] so bright that it almost hurt to look at. Everyone, it seemed, was trying to say something about themselves.

Breakfast was a [[struggle]]. His mum had made pancakes, his [[favourite]], yet he could only [[manage]] half of one. The kitchen smelled of [[butter]] and fresh coffee. Usually that smell made him happy. This morning it made him feel slightly [[sick]]. Three times he checked his bag. Pencil case, water bottle, timetable, and a brand-new [[calculator]] that he had no idea how to use.

For a few seconds, he watched without [[moving]]. He could see the bright reception area through the glass: [[polished]] floors, noticeboards [[crowded]] with photographs, and a tall display of paper leaves covered in names. Behind him, the [[pavement]] continued to fill. Each pause made him more aware of the space he [[occupied]], so he took a breath, tightened his [[grip]] on his bag and stepped towards the door.

For a moment, he simply stopped. People [[flowed]] around him as if he were a [[rock]] in a river. Everyone else seemed to know exactly where they were going. His throat felt [[tight]]. A small, [[embarrassing]] part of him wanted to turn around, walk back through the gates and go home to his [[quiet]] kitchen. Nobody would [[notice]], would they? Nobody here even knew his name.

He chose a seat by the window, next to a boy with [[messy]] red hair and a backpack covered in [[badges]]. The boy gave him a small, [[shy]] smile. Leo smiled back. Outside, the mist was [[lifting]], and pale sunshine was spilling across the playing [[fields]]. His stomach was still [[fluttering]], but the feeling had changed. It no longer felt like fear. It felt, quite possibly, like the beginning of something.

He crossed the doorway. The change was small: one step out of the [[corridor]] and into the classroom. Yet the noise behind him [[softened]], and the room’s quieter sounds came forward: a chair shifting, a pencil rolling across a desk, [[pages]] turning. Leo’s [[worries]] did not disappear. Still, as he chose a seat and set down his bag, they made room for something else—a [[cautious]] sense that the day had begun, and that he had [[managed]] its first step.

He followed the [[nearest]] group, hoping the [[flow]] of students would carry him towards the correct classroom. Instead, they turned sharply through a doorway and disappeared. Leo stopped beside a row of blue [[lockers]], where a younger student knelt to [[fasten]] a loose shoelace. On the wall, a large map showed the school’s different floors, but the tiny [[labels]] seemed to [[swim]] before his eyes.

He noticed small details as he waited: a [[strip]] of green paint scratched from a locker [[handle]], a paper star taped crookedly to a classroom door, the [[shine]] of sunlight on a window at the end of the corridor. These [[ordinary]] things [[steadied]] him. He could not yet understand the school, but he could look at one part at a time, letting the [[rush]] of bodies pass around him.

His heart still beat too quickly. He felt [[excited]], but the excitement was [[tangled]] with worry: the fear of [[entering]] the wrong room, forgetting his [[timetable]], or being the only person without a friend. The thought of turning back crossed his mind. Then the bell sounded again, and the crowd began to move with greater [[purpose]]. Standing still no longer felt like an [[option]].

His uniform felt [[stiff]]. The white shirt was [[tucked]] tightly into dark trousers, and the [[collar]] rubbed his neck whenever he turned his head. A new pair of black shoes [[shone]] beneath the morning light, although their hard edges pressed against his [[heels]]. Around him, students wore the same school colours in different ways: untidy ties, neat jumpers, skirts with thick [[tights]], and jackets pulled over uniforms against the cold.

If the playground had been noisy, the corridors were pure [[chaos]]. Lockers banged open and slammed shut. Teachers with [[lanyards]] and coffee mugs tried to [[direct]] the traffic, pointing and waving like police officers at a busy [[junction]]. Students pushed past in every direction. Some walked in tight, [[chatty]] groups; others moved alone, heads down and [[headphones]] on.

Leo looked down at his own clothes. Navy jumper, grey [[trousers]], sensible black shoes. His mum had chosen them. Next to the girl in glittery trainers, or the boy whose [[hoodie]] was covered in [[cartoon]] dinosaurs, he felt painfully [[ordinary]]. Some kids obviously cared deeply about [[fashion]]. Others had simply [[grabbed]] the first thing on their bedroom floor. Where, he wondered, did he fit?

Leo [[unfolded]] his timetable, smoothing its [[creased]] edges against his palm. Room 12 was on the first floor. He found the [[staircase]] and climbed it, listening to the noise change as he rose. The lower corridor was full of movement; above, the air seemed [[calmer]], though footsteps still hurried along the [[landing]]. Light from the tall windows fell across the steps in long, [[pale]] shapes.

Noise filled the corridor from wall to wall. Shoes tapped and [[squeaked]] against the floor; lockers clanged shut, and chair [[legs]] scraped somewhere behind an open classroom door. Bags brushed against [[coats]] as students [[squeezed]] past each other. Their voices blended into a busy [[hum]], rising and fading like [[waves]]. Leo could not separate the sounds, yet each one seemed to remind him that everyone else knew where to go.

Outside, the September air was cool and [[damp]]. A thin [[mist]] hung over the rooftops, while every passing car [[hissed]] through the [[puddles]] left by last night’s rain. Leo walked quickly.
